title: Motion in a Plane — NIOS Official Summary
intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Physics (312) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 4: Motion in a Plane. It covers projectile motion (constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration), the projectile formulas for maximum height, time of flight, range and trajectory, uniform circular motion, centripetal acceleration and force, and applications such as banking of roads and aircraft in vertical loops.

branches.label: Projectile Formulas
details: Time of flight T = 2v₀ sin θ / g

branches.label: Circular Motion
details: Movement along the circumference of a circle

sections.heading: Projectile Motion
bullets: Projectile motion is motion which has constant velocity in a certain direction and constant acceleration in a direction perpendicular to that of the velocity.
The two important properties of projectile motion are: (i) a constant horizontal velocity component, and (ii) a constant vertically downward acceleration component.
When air resistance is neglected, these two components govern the motion entirely.

sections.heading: Maximum Height, Time of Flight and Range
bullets: Maximum height: at the instant when the projectile is at its maximum height, the vertical component of its velocity is zero. h = v₀² sin² θ / (2g).
Time of flight: the total time for which the projectile is in the air. It is the time interval between the instant of launch and the instant when it hits the ground. T = 2 v₀ sin θ / g.

Range: the horizontal distance the projectile covers from launch to landing. The path of any projectile launched at an angle to the horizontal is a parabola or a portion of a parabola. R = v₀² sin 2θ / g.
Trajectory: y = y₀ + (tan θ)(x − x₀) − [g / (2 (v₀ cos θ)²)] (x − x₀)².

sections.heading: Circular Motion
bullets: Circular motion is the movement of an object along the circumference of a circle (or along a circular path).
Average velocity in circular motion is v_avg = Δr / Δt.
Uniform circular motion is motion with constant speed in a circle. The instantaneous velocity is v = lim(Δt → 0) Δr / Δt and is always tangential to the circle.

sections.heading: Centripetal Acceleration and Force
bullets: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration directed toward the centre of the circle in uniform circular motion: a = v² / r.
Using v = rω (where ω is the angular speed), we can write a = ω² r.
Centripetal force is F = m v² / r, equivalently F = m r ω². It is the net inward force needed to keep a body in uniform circular motion.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity — in uniform circular motion the direction of velocity is changing continuously even though the speed is constant.

An important thing to understand: the term 'centripetal force' does not refer to a type of force of interaction like the force of gravitation or electrical force. It refers to the NET inward force, whatever its physical origin.

sections.heading: Applications of Uniform Circular Motion
bullets: Banking of roads: at a banked road of angle θ, the normal force has a horizontal component that contributes to the centripetal force. F_N sin θ = m v² / r and F_N cos θ = m g, giving θ = tan⁻¹(v² / (r g)).
Aircraft in vertical loops: at the bottom of a vertical loop the normal force on a passenger is N = m (g + v² / r) — heavier than their weight.

Other applications: orbits of satellites (gravity supplies the centripetal force), centrifuges (separating substances by density), and turning vehicles on flat roads (where friction provides the centripetal force).

key_takeaways: Projectile motion has a constant horizontal velocity component and a constant vertically downward acceleration component (gravity).
For a projectile launched at speed v₀ and angle θ on level ground: maximum height h = v₀² sin² θ / (2g), time of flight T = 2 v₀ sin θ / g, range R = v₀² sin 2θ / g.
The trajectory of a projectile is a parabola.
Uniform circular motion is accelerated motion: centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = ω²r is directed toward the centre.
Centripetal force F = mv²/r is the net inward force; it is not a new kind of force — its source is tension, gravity, friction, normal force, etc.
Banking of roads (angle θ given by tan θ = v²/rg) allows vehicles to negotiate curves at higher speeds; aircraft in vertical loops experience a normal force m(g + v²/r) at the bottom of the loop.

glossary.definition: A body thrown into the air and subsequently moving under the action of gravity alone (air resistance neglected).

Motion that has constant velocity in one direction and constant acceleration perpendicular to that velocity. For a body thrown near Earth, the horizontal velocity is constant and the vertical acceleration is g downward.
The path traced by a moving particle. For an ideal projectile, the trajectory is a parabola.
The highest point of a projectile's trajectory; h = v₀² sin² θ / (2g) for launch speed v₀ and angle θ.
The total time the projectile remains in the air; T = 2 v₀ sin θ / g on level ground.
The horizontal distance the projectile travels from launch to landing on the same horizontal level; R = v₀² sin 2θ / g.
Motion of an object along the circumference of a circle (or any circular path).
Circular motion at constant speed. The velocity vector is always tangent to the circle and changes direction continuously.
Acceleration directed toward the centre of a circle in uniform circular motion: a = v² / r = ω² r.
The net inward force required for uniform circular motion: F = mv²/r = mrω². Its physical source can be tension, gravity, friction, or a normal force — not a new kind of force.
Tilting of a road at a curve so that the normal force provides part of the centripetal force. The banking angle satisfies tan θ = v²/(rg).
